modelterms7

Model terms as S7 objects. A term is the recipe that a formula names: the mapping from a data frame to a design-matrix block, the penalty attached to the block’s coefficients, and the metadata that a fit uses: coefficient names, hyperparameters with their links, whether the penalized objective is differentiable, and how effective degrees of freedom are counted.

The package is part of the statmodels7 toolkit.

Installation 

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("statmodels7/modelterms7")

The terms

An additive term contributes a block of columns, so the predictor is η=∑tXtβt\eta = \sum_t X_t \beta_t and a penalized fit minimizes −ℓ(β)+∑tρt(βt;θt)-\ell(\beta) + \sum_t \rho_t(\beta_t; \theta_t):

  • linpar() is the unpenalized parametric block;
  • ridge(), lasso(), scad(), mcp() and enet() attach the corresponding penalties7 object to their block;
  • random() builds grouped intercepts and slopes with the effect distribution as the penalty: a multivariate one lets the effects of a group depend on each other, and its matrix parameter carries the dependence on whichever parameters7 chart is given to it; a second bar labels effects that share a covariance block with those of other terms;
  • s() and te() are the penalized smooths of one and of several covariates, built on basis7;
  • nl() carries a contribution that is nonlinear in its own parameters, and its block is the Jacobian, which is refreshed as the parameters move;
  • seg(), jump() and jseg() estimate the break-points at which an effect changes slope, level, or both, and seg_start() chooses where the iteration begins.

A structural term rewrites the likelihood instead of adding to the predictor: gas() gives score-driven dynamics and regime() a latent Markov chain. Both return their exact derivative alongside the state, because the recursion is the only place where that derivative can be computed.

A structural term has parameters of its own instead of coefficients, and it declares them. They are estimated on the unconstrained scale of each one’s own chart, so a persistence stays stationary and a loading stays positive for every value that the optimizer proposes.

g <- gas(p = 1, q = 1)
term_params(g)
#> [1] "omega"  "kappa1" "pacf1"
vapply(term_links(g), function(l) l@link_name, character(1))
#>      omega     kappa1      pacf1 
#> "identity"      "log"   "rhobit"

cens() is not a term. It marks a censored response on the left side of a formula, and interpret_formula() returns it as the response. statmodels7::statmod() and rstatmod() reject a censored response, because a censored likelihood for it is not yet implemented.

A term’s own parameters take formulas

A term that has parameters of its own (nl(), seg(), jump(), jseg() and gas()) can develop each of them over covariates by a two-sided formula whose left side names the parameter. The development acts on the unconstrained scale of that parameter’s chart, so the constraint holds at every observation and not merely on average. Examples are a break-point with a random effect for each group and a loading that depends on a covariate.

pan <- data.frame(x = runif(60), id = factor(rep(1:6, each = 10)))
pan$y <- rnorm(60)

sg <- term_build(seg(x, psi ~ random(~ 1 | id)), pan)
term_coef_names(sg)[1:4]
#> [1] "seg.beta"             "seg.gamma1"           "seg.psi1.(Intercept)"
#> [4] "seg.psi1.random.1"

This is the random-changepoint model, and it needs no separate term. The same route carries a penalty: nl(~ a * exp(-r * x), a ~ 0 + ridge(~ g)) puts a ridge on the amplitudes across the levels of g, and term_penalties() reports every entry that a term declares, with the subset of its parameters that each entry covers.

Effects that share a covariance block

A second bar labels a random effect, following brms: in ~ 1 + x | u | id the last position is the grouping variable, and the middle one is a label shared by the terms whose effects are correlated with each other. R nests bars to the left, so the parser yields that reading. The label is a name and is never evaluated, so a column of the data with the same name is not read.

tm <- random(~ 1 + x | u | id)
term_tag(tm)
#> [1] "u"
term_penalties(term_build(tm, pan))
#> list()

The empty list is the intended result. The coefficients of a labelled term share a block with those of every other term that carries the label, and that block may span another equation, so the fitting layer builds the prior over the whole block. statmodels7 collects the terms with the same label, so y ~ random(~ 1 | u | id) | sigma ~ random(~ 1 | u | id) is a random intercept in the mean correlated with a random intercept in the scale.

Break-points three ways

A break-point term estimates the positions in one of three ways. The default uses the working fits of Muggeo for seg() and of Fasola, Muggeo and Kuchenhoff for jump() and jseg().

smoothed = replaces the absolute value inside the term with a numericals7 abs_smoother, and each break-point then becomes an ordinary parameter of a differentiable model. term_jacobian_block() shows the difference. The block of seg() is already a Jacobian, because the construction is continuous. The two discontinuous constructions read their position off a product of the fitted coefficients, so their block is a working linearization with a frozen weight until the term is smoothed.

jb <- function(...) term_jacobian_block(term_build(jump(x, ...), pan))
c(sharp    = jb(npsi = 1),
  smoothed = jb(npsi = 1, smoothed = numericals7::smooth_probit()))
#>    sharp smoothed 
#>    FALSE     TRUE

The same difference determines which developments a discontinuous term accepts. On a sharp jump() or jseg() the estimated coefficients are products of the change of level and the development, so a penalty on the development would act on the product, and the term rejects a development that carries a penalty. A development without a penalty is accepted, and a smoothed term accepts both kinds, because its block is a Jacobian.

marginal = TRUE, together with a subformula psi ~ random(~ 1 | g), integrates the latent break-point of each group out of the likelihood. The prior’s parameters are then estimated by maximum likelihood, and the positions are not parameters of the fit. For jump() the sum over the positions is exact: the process of active break-points is a hidden Markov chain over the side patterns, so for a group of nn observations and KK break-points the forward recursion costs nK2KnK2^K where the sum over the cells costs (n+1)K(n+1)^K. The continuous kinds, seg() and jseg(), integrate one break-point per group by Gauss-Kronrod quadrature on each interval between the group’s ordered observations.

Simulating from a term

term_simulate() is the function through which statmodels7::rstatmod() draws a response from a term that carries state. A score-driven filter does not need a second recursion for this. The filter evaluates its score once per observation, in time order, at the predictor that it has just produced, so a callback that draws the response at that predictor and returns the score of the drawn value turns the filter into a generator. A latent chain draws its path from the stationary distribution that the likelihood uses for the initial state, since any other start would simulate a different model. A term without state has nothing of its own to draw, and the base method signals an error.

A formula, interpreted

The interpreter evaluates each call in the formula and treats it as a term when the value inherits from model_term. A term class defined outside the package therefore works in a formula without registration.

dd <- data.frame(y = rnorm(50), x1 = rnorm(50), x2 = rnorm(50),
                 g = factor(sample(letters[1:5], 50, TRUE)))
dd$L <- matrix(rnorm(50 * 3), 50, 3)

out <- interpret_formula(y ~ x1 + log(abs(x2)) + lasso(L) +
                           random(~ 1 | g), dd)
names(out$terms)
#> [1] "linpar"         "lasso(L)"       "random(~1 | g)"

x1 and log(abs(x2)) collapse into one linpar block: a bare covariate is a covariate of that block, and so is a call whose value is not a term. A call whose evaluation fails signals an error that names the call.

built <- lapply(out$terms, term_build, data = dd)
vapply(built, term_npar, integer(1))
#>         linpar       lasso(L) random(~1 | g) 
#>              3              3              5
vapply(built, term_smooth, logical(1))
#>         linpar       lasso(L) random(~1 | g) 
#>           TRUE          FALSE           TRUE

term_smooth() is computed from the kink set of the term’s penalty and is not a property of the term. The lasso block therefore reports FALSE, and a fitting layer can use the answer to select the terms that need a non-smooth method.

What a built term carries 

sm <- term_build(s(x1, basis7::bspline_smooth(k = 8)), dd)
dim(term_matrix(sm))
#> [1] 50  7
term_coef_names(sm)
#> [1] "s(x1).lin" "s(x1).z1"  "s(x1).z2"  "s(x1).z3"  "s(x1).z4"  "s(x1).z5" 
#> [7] "s(x1).z6"
term_penalty(sm)@params
#> [1] "lambda"

Every built term also carries a blueprint that reproduces the mapping on new data. Prediction reapplies the factor levels, contrasts and knot placement recorded at build time and does not derive them again from the new rows.

newdd <- dd[1:5, ]
identical(term_predict(sm, newdd), term_matrix(sm)[1:5, ])
#> [1] TRUE

check_term() validates an additive term against a data frame: the shape and names of the block, that prediction on the same data reproduces the block, and that prediction on a subset equals the corresponding rows. A term that rebuilds its encoding on new rows instead of reapplying its blueprint fails the last check.

res <- check_term(linpar(~ x1 + g), dd, verbose = FALSE)
all(res$status == "OK")
#> [1] TRUE

edf() computes effective degrees of freedom from the quantities that a fit supplies. An unpenalized block counts its columns, a smooth penalty counts tr⁡[(H+S)−1H]\operatorname{tr}[(H + S)^{-1} H], with HH the unpenalized curvature and SS the Hessian of the penalty, and a kinked penalty (the lasso, the elastic net, SCAD and MCP) counts the nonzero coefficients.
